Who made the IR Worldview Inventory, how it was built, and how to reach the project.

People can agree on what should happen and disagree about why. They can also apply different standards to a military crisis, an export restriction or the release of a powerful AI model. I built this app to make those differences easier to examine.

The questionnaires cover international politics, Security, Technology and AI Governance. The Library explains the arguments behind the results. Cases let you work through a particular decision, while AI Futures explores the conditions you would accept in very different possible worlds.
You can start with whichever subject interests you. The aim is to leave with a clearer explanation of your choices and a question worth discussing with someone else.

. I studied international relations at Johns Hopkins SAIS, with a focus on technology and governance. I began this as a personal project and used AI tools extensively to build it. The design and interpretations have changed through successive rounds of testing, criticism and revision.
This is an independent project. The scoring rules are available in
, together with their limitations. Empirical validation remains work to do.

A misleading question or an explanation that does not follow from your answers is useful feedback. Please name the page or question when contacting me. You do not need to include your result link or disclose your answers.

Two governments exchange the same security guarantee. Ask whether they understand one another as partners or adversaries, then consider how that relationship changes the promise's meaning. A signature alone cannot establish a shared identity.

A government receives a cheap offer for digital infrastructure. Ask who can change the financing terms, restrict access to knowledge or deny future upgrades. The initial price cannot settle whether the government will retain useful alternatives.

Limits, privacy, and corrections

How much weight do you give to rivalry, uncertainty about intentions, and positional competition among major powers? High scores lean toward the view that security competition is a durable constraint. Low scores suggest skepticism that rivalry is the main organizing logic.

Do you think rules, monitoring, and repeated interaction can make cooperation more durable even without a world government? High scores lean institutionalist. Low scores suggest you see institutions mostly as mirrors of power.

How much do coalitions, regime type, bureaucratic capacity, and transnational actors shape foreign policy relative to external pressure? This dimension captures whether you think states facing similar environments can still behave differently for domestic reasons.

Do legitimacy, recognition, and social meaning help shape interests and threats, or are they mostly rhetorical cover for material interests? High scores lean constructivist. Low scores suggest skepticism that norms have much independent force.

How central are production, finance, trade dependence, sanctions, and leverage to your explanation of world politics? High scores mean you keep political economy firmly in view. They do not, by themselves, make you a critical political economist.
When a major power has room to press for advantage, is the safer instinct to hold back or to exploit the opening? This is a strategic style dimension, not a standalone worldview family.
When sovereignty and wider moral obligations clash, which usually carries more weight in your judgment? This is a normative style dimension, not a claim about who is more moral.
The foundation result is a seven-dimension profile. This is the main output. It shows which lines of argument you lean toward and where you are mixed.
One or two IR traditions are shown as interpretive shorthand for that profile. They are labels for a pattern, not natural kinds or permanent identities.
Strategic and normative style
The result also reports a strategic style and a normative style. These modifiers sit alongside the profile. They are not separate worldview families.
Security and Technology Focus Areas produce separate records from concrete issue files. Their domain scales are not translated onto the Foundation or combined into a master score.
Second-choice answers count at reduced weight

In Advanced mode, tradeoff and mini-case questions let you pick a second-choice answer after your primary. That secondary answer is scored at 45% of the weight of your primary pick. This reflects the intuition that a genuine second choice is a softer signal than a clear primary commitment, but it is not derived from a validated weighting experiment. It is an authored judgment.
Family weights are authored reference profiles

The four authored tradition reference points used to identify the closest tradition-level fit are realism, institutionalism, constructivism, and critical political economy. They are stylized summaries built from editorial judgment about what each tradition centrally holds. They are not derived from a sample of scholars or validated against an external standard. The closest modeled fit is an interpretive shorthand, not a certified diagnosis.
Focus Area results are separate records, not Foundation measurements

Focus Area results come from issue-specific questions and are reported on their own domain scales. They sit beside the Foundation and do not rescore its seven dimensions or archetype. There is no numeric bridge and no master score combining the records.
This is not a validated psychometric instrument. The dimensions, family profiles, and thresholds reflect theoretical judgment and editorial design, not large-sample calibration.

Realism, institutionalism, constructivism, and critical political economy are modeled here as simplified reference profiles. The inventory preserves issue-specific combinations instead of forcing every answer into one tradition.
Political economy is not a catch-all

The model distinguishes broad political-economy salience from a stronger critical or systemic commitment. Thinking economics matters does not automatically make someone a Critical Political Economy result.
Focus Areas are separate
Focus Areas are meant to surface domain-specific instinct, not to masquerade as extra scientific precision. Their readouts are kept separate from the Foundation result.
Scores are relative, not absolute
A score of 5.4 on a dimension means you lean that way within this model's scale. It does not mean 54% of people agree with you, and it is not a percentile.

The current model does not fully represent several important traditions, including feminist IR, postcolonial theory, and green IR. People anchored in those traditions may be mapped onto the nearest modeled family instead.

How this inventory works
This editorial questionnaire compares your answers across seven foreign-policy tradeoffs. It shows which arguments recur and where your judgments pull in different directions.
What the result means
Read the profile first. Tradition names provide concise references for nearby patterns across the seven dimensions.
What it can tell you

The IR Worldview Inventory is best read as an editorially designed interpretation tool. It asks which arguments you tend to find more convincing, where your instincts cluster, and where they pull in different directions.
The result summarizes your answers. It has not been validated as a scientific diagnostic or a measure of expertise, and it does not identify a permanent personality type.
This editorial questionnaire has not been validated as a scientific instrument.
Tradition labels are shorthand for a multidimensional profile.
Mixed outputs show where your answers draw on more than one modeled tradition.
No score is a population percentile or population ranking.
How to read the four result layers
Who it is for

The main audience is people who think seriously about foreign policy, international order, or strategic affairs: students, practitioners, researchers, and engaged readers. Some IR background helps, but the main prompts are written in plain English rather than specialist jargon.
It can also work as a classroom or discussion tool. The value is often in seeing where you expected one tradition label but the profile itself points somewhere more mixed.
Why Focus Area records stay separate

Broad priors and domain-specific instincts are related, but they are not the same thing. Someone can hold a generally institutionalist foundation profile and still lean toward deterrence-heavy arguments in a Security Focus Area. Someone else can read world politics through power and rivalry in the abstract but still resist escalation in a concrete case.
That is why the inventory keeps the Foundation result separate from Focus Area records. Focus Areas show how a profile travels into live arguments. They do not add points to the core classification.

Focus Area questions do three different jobs. Explanation cards ask what best explains a case. Decision cards ask what should carry the most weight in response. Actor-lens cards ask what logic would look strongest from that actor's own position, and are tracked separately so perspective-modeling does not overwrite your own judgment.
In shared Foundation links, the Foundation profile, closest traditions, and style outputs travel with the result. Focus Area interpretation is treated as a separate applied readout.
Why these issue areas

The focus-area structure is loosely inspired by how international affairs programs, including the SAIS MAIR curriculum, often group issue areas. This project is independent and does not imply affiliation or endorsement.
Foundation forms and the research-comparison block

New Foundation runs start with the core. The optional baseline extension keeps the scored questions in their existing order and omits the separate research-comparison battery. That battery includes U.S.-specific statements drawn from a published foreign-policy scale; it does not contribute to the worldview result.

Saved full-extension drafts keep their original questions and totals. You can continue that form or explicitly restart. Results retain their exact form, so the old and new administrations remain distinguishable. Identical scored answers produce identical scores; that does not show that people would answer identically after a change in context or burden.
How answers become a profile
The Foundation combines seven dimensions. Scoring and labels translate those values into a readable profile without turning the output into a permanent type.

Scoring begins with the foundation questions. Some items are plain-language agreement prompts, while others are tradeoffs or mini-cases. Together they map onto the same seven dimensions and are averaged into a seven-dimension profile on a 1 to 7 scale.

The model then compares that profile with four stylized tradition profiles: realism, institutionalism, constructivism, and critical political economy. The closest one or two are shown as interpretive shorthand.
Strategic and normative style are reported separately from the restraint and order-versus-justice dimensions. They help describe the profile, but they do not create a new worldview family.
Focus Area scores are issue-specific. Actor-lens responses are stored and shown, but they do not quietly become your main Focus Area read the way a normal own-judgment answer would.

High political-economy salience does not automatically force a Critical Political Economy result. A stronger critical or systemic pattern is required before that tradition becomes the primary shorthand.

The foundation profile is built from seven dimensions drawn from major debates in IR. They are meant to capture broad explanatory priors and style differences without pretending to measure everything that matters.
Which choices are authored
Three aspects of the scoring model involve explicit editorial choices that are not derived from calibration data. Naming them plainly is part of honest instrument design.
How Perspective Runs work
Each Perspective Run answer adds a predefined change to one or more Foundation dimensions. The result compares those adjusted scores with your saved baseline.
The saved Foundation remains your baseline. Perspective Runs do not assign another worldview family or feed points back into Foundation scoring.
Small differences should be read lightly. The result names the scenario responsible for the largest change and the dimensions that stayed close to the baseline.
Why the wording is plain English
The prompts aim to be readable without prior theory training. Technical language lives in optional explainers, not in the main question stem.
Jargon-heavy prompts can reward prior training instead of revealing the judgment the question is meant to test. Plain language reduces that problem and makes disagreement easier to interpret.
Maps and public-position records are editorial reference layers. Their construction, support, and limits remain visible rather than borrowing certainty from the scoring system.

The Foundation robustness diagnostic uses constructed answer sets, not human participants. It reruns the live scorer and result resolver after the smallest permitted answer changes, forced-choice substitutions, and defined omission and neutralisation probes. This is a deterministic structural-sensitivity diagnostic.

Results changed more often near family boundaries and the boundary between a single-family and blended reading. The correlated synthetic and canonical ensembles changed less often when their starting results were farther from those boundaries.

The diagnostic supports no claim about reliability, validity, or population distributions. The exact methods, seeds, protected-file digests, and generated data are available in the project repository.

The posture sign uses 4 as a registered raw-score boundary. Four is not the constructed null center for every form. For the exact full form, the registered independent-null calibration centers restraint at 4.657735. The authored forced-choice signals make that form asymmetric around the raw boundary, so equal numeric distances on either side of 4 should not be read as equivalent positions around the form's constructed center.

How the Worldview Map is built

The reference matrix is the default view. Its columns are Power, Rules, Meaning, and Structure; its rows are applying advantage and restraint. The eight cells hold the eight pure Foundation archetypes. An exact saved Foundation payload marks one cell for a pure result or two cells in the same row for a blend.

The secondary continuous view has a horizontal axis from power and competition to rules and institutions, and a vertical axis from material and economic structure to ideas and norms. Each Foundation value is centered on the neutral score of 4, multiplied by an authored weight, and added to its axis. The two sums are divided by fixed spread constants and limited to the range from −1 to 1. This normalization is an editorial construction, not an estimate from a population.

Eligible personal baselines and Perspective Runs use those coefficients. Decision Patterns and evidence-coded reference positions use the same projection as contextual overlays. Restraint is not part of either axis, so this view cannot distinguish the two matrix postures. Realism, Institutionalism, and Critical political economy all include material explanations, so the vertical axis separates those references only weakly.
The continuous view supports orientation and side-by-side reading. Screen distance is not calibrated; it measures neither ideological difference nor uncertainty.

Decision Patterns use authored fingerprints. Low, medium, and high levels become 2.5, 4, and 5.5 on the internal Foundation scale. Dimensions absent from a pattern fingerprint use the midpoint of 4 for projection. Decision Pattern marks are authored editorial examples; no population sample underlies them.
How thinkers and public positions are coded

Thinkers and public positions summarize public postures from a dated source ledger. Each record carries an evidence window, dimension-level support, dispute notes, dated updates, and a second-person review before publication.

A public reading card needs support on at least five Foundation dimensions. A map position requires linked evidence on all seven dimensions because the projection consumes all seven values. Missing values remain missing, and the profile stays off the map.

The internal coding stores values on the Foundation's 1–7 scale. The public default view shows support levels, coding notes, sources, and disputes while keeping the coefficients hidden. Strong support requires linked evidence from at least two source records.
AI-governance profiles use the separate AI Governance axes and their own visualization. Values from the two instruments are never merged into a single coordinate.

Connections and pair comparisons

Connected Profile uses three authored rules: access and control, public authority and practical capacity, and cooperation under security conditions. Each observation retains its subject, original result, question or score, and completion details. Actor-role judgments cannot establish a personal choice. A named result cannot supply missing answers.

Pair comparisons subtract scores only within the same registered bank, scorer, form, language and wording edition. There is no reviewed mapping across different forms or languages. Unknown completion details stay unknown; people may explicitly supply original completion details in Compare. AI links omit the form and cannot recover it from scores.

Differences below 0.35 on a 1–7 scale are described as small. Directional wording requires both positions to sit at least 0.35 away from the midpoint. These are editorial display rules, not statistical significance, validated equivalence or population norms. Exact largest-gap ties are retained. No scores are pooled across subjects.

Foundation answer examples require an exact completion identifier and matching questionnaire, scoring, wording and language details. An unavailable example may reflect deletion, a different language, missing answers or missing completion binding; it does not establish the age of the result. Authored alternative answers are distinguished from recorded second choices. Comparison terms use the registered scorer, with rounding residuals retained in its calculation.

New pair inputs, display names, corrections and follow-up reflections remain in page memory and clear on leaving or resetting. New comparisons do not fetch pasted links or create joint share links. Historical Compare URLs already send their query contents to the server when opened; later address-bar cleanup cannot undo that exposure.

The inventory states where interpretation stops, explains what generated links contain, and gives factual, privacy, and security problems a narrow correction route.

Privacy and data use
Your drafts and saved history stay in this browser

The inventory requires no account. Saved results and Current Case judgments support your Profile on this device. Generating a result creates a URL that encodes the data needed to reopen it; the Sharing section explains that boundary. When coarse measurement is enabled, the separate aggregate counters described below receive derived buckets. Draft answers and saved histories stay outside those counters. The site does not collect research responses.

The site does not ask for consent to a study, collect research responses, or connect contact details to quiz results. A future study would need separate information about its purpose, data, consent, retention, deletion, security, and access rules before collection could begin.

Separate first-party aggregate counters record each Foundation step reached. On result generation, they also receive derived score and label buckets plus each item ID and a coarse response-time bucket. These counters receive no answers, raw timestamps, response ordering, respondent or session identifier, credentials, or referrer.

Vercel Web Analytics receives a small set of named interactions. Automatic pageview tracking is not installed. The only custom properties are a published Current Case ID when relevant, broad route category, device class, referrer category, and broad return-age bucket.

Full URLs, result payloads, answer IDs, confidence, reasoning tags, profile families, saved-result flags, dimension scores, email, free text, custom timestamps, and app-owned persistent IP records are excluded. Referrer URLs are reduced to categories in the browser. The analytics request does not include request IP, cookie, user-agent, or referrer headers.

To limit aggregate-counter abuse, the write endpoint converts the request IP into a process-salted, one-way bucket key. Neither the IP nor that key is written to the aggregate database. The key stays only in server memory and expires with the server process.
A first-seen UTC date stays in this browser to create the return-age bucket. It is not sent as an identifier and is deleted when you opt out or delete local history.

Foundation, AI, module, Perspective, and shared Profile links encode the data needed to reopen the shared view. A Focus Area result link includes its answer selections; other result types may encode derived scores, labels, or saved layers. Opening or sharing one of these URLs exposes that encoded data to the recipient and to services that handle the request. Treat those URLs as disclosures you control. Removing local history does not retract a link already sent or remove it from browser or message history.

Ordinary Current Case links contain no answer. You may explicitly add your final reading to native share or copied text. A case invitation contains no judgment from the sender; both readers complete the case before comparing their answers directly.

The contact route is limited to factual corrections, privacy questions, and security reports. Correspondence is not automatically linked to a result, Profile, Current Case response, or analytics event.

References | IR Worldview Inventory
Selected bibliography for the IR Worldview Inventory, with primary texts and foundational works by tradition.
History of the Peloponnesian War
Various translations. Recommended: Strassler ed., The Landmark Thucydides (Free Press, 1996).
The original source for realist intuitions about fear, honor, and interest as drivers of conflict. The Melian Dialogue remains the clearest statement of power-over-principle logic.
Politics Among Nations: The Struggle for Power and Peace
Alfred A. Knopf. Sixth edition revised by Kenneth W. Thompson (McGraw-Hill, 1985).
Classical realism's foundational text. Grounds the argument in a concept of the national interest defined in terms of power. Still the best statement of statecraft as a discipline.
Theory of International Politics
Addison-Wesley. Reissued by McGraw-Hill.

The founding text of structural realism (neorealism). Shifts the causal argument from human nature to the architecture of the system: anarchy and the distribution of capabilities. Sets the terms for most subsequent theoretical debate.
https://www.waveland.com/browse.php?t=144
Man, the State and War

Introduces the three-image framework for understanding the causes of war: human nature, the state, and the structure of the international system. Required background for understanding what structural realism is reacting against.
The Tragedy of Great Power Politics
W. W. Norton. Updated edition 2014.
The clearest statement of offensive realism. Argues that anarchy compels states to maximize power because there is no safe stopping point. China's rise, he argues, will not be peaceful.
Perception and Misperception in International Politics
The essential text on how cognitive biases and the security dilemma interact. Bridges classical realism and the psychology of strategic decision-making.
War and Change in World Politics
A structural account of how hegemonic transitions produce conflict. Relevant to contemporary US-China dynamics and to the question of whether power transitions are inherently destabilizing.
After Hegemony: Cooperation and Discord in the World Political Economy

The central text of liberal institutionalism. Argues that international regimes can sustain cooperation even after the dominant power that created them declines, contrary to the realist expectation that order depends on hegemony.
Keohane, Robert O. and Nye, Joseph S.
Little, Brown. Fourth edition, Longman, 2011.

Introduces complex interdependence as an alternative to realist assumptions: multiple channels of contact, no hierarchy of issues, and limits on the effectiveness of military force. A key bridge between realism and institutionalism.
Diplomacy and Domestic Politics: The Logic of Two-Level Games
International Organization, vol. 42, no. 3.

Argues that international negotiations are simultaneously domestic political contests. Win-sets, the range of agreements that can survive ratification, shape what is achievable abroad. One of the most cited articles in IR.
After Victory: Institutions, Strategic Restraint, and the Rebuilding of Order After Major Wars
Explains why post-war hegemons sometimes bind themselves through institutions rather than simply imposing order. Relevant to debates about whether US-led liberal order is durable.
The Evolution of Cooperation
Uses iterated prisoner's dilemma to show how cooperation can emerge among self-interested actors without central authority. The game-theoretic foundation for much institutionalist reasoning.
The False Promise of International Institutions
International Security, vol. 19, no. 3.

A sharp realist challenge to institutionalism. Argues that institutions reflect the interests of powerful states and cannot independently cause peace. Essential reading for understanding what institutionalism is up against.
Anarchy Is What States Make of It: The Social Construction of Power Politics
International Organization, vol. 46, no. 2.

The article that established constructivism as a mainstream IR approach. Argues that anarchy has no single fixed logic because its consequences depend on the identities and relationships states construct. Directly challenges Waltz.
Social Theory of International Politics

The full theoretical treatment. Distinguishes three cultures of anarchy (Hobbesian, Lockean, Kantian) and argues that state identities are both constructed and capable of change through sustained interaction.
Katzenstein, Peter J. (ed.)
The Culture of National Security: Norms and Identity in World Politics
A landmark collection applying constructivist ideas to security policy empirically. Contributors examine how norms shaped German rearmament, Japanese security policy, and US nuclear doctrine.
Finnemore, Martha and Sikkink, Kathryn
International Norm Dynamics and Political Change
International Organization, vol. 52, no. 4.
Introduces the norm life cycle from emergence to cascade to internalization, and explains how norms spread and gain causal force. The most cited constructivist article on norm diffusion.
The Promise of Constructivism in International Relations Theory
International Security, vol. 23, no. 1.
A clear critical overview distinguishing conventional and critical constructivism. Useful entry point for understanding the range of positions within the tradition.
Mearsheimer, John J. and Walt, Stephen M.
Leaving Theory Behind: Why Simplistic Hypothesis Testing Is Bad for International Relations
European Journal of International Relations, vol. 19, no. 3.
Not primarily a constructivism critique, but includes a sharp challenge to the empirical research program constructivism has produced. A useful counterpoint for evaluating constructivist claims.
Blackwell. Second edition, Pinter, 1994.

Argues that structural power, through control over production, finance, security, and knowledge, creates political authority independent of formal state power. The sharpest introduction to international political economy as a distinct field.
Social Forces, States and World Orders: Beyond International Relations Theory
Millennium: Journal of International Studies, vol. 10, no. 2.

The founding text of neo-Gramscian IPE. Argues that theory always serves someone's interests and that hegemony operates as much through ideas and institutions as through force. 'Problem-solving theory versus critical theory' is a central distinction.
The Political Economy of International Relations
A survey of the three main approaches to IPE, nationalism, liberalism, and Marxism, through major policy debates. Useful background for understanding where critical PE positions itself.
The Economic Development of Latin America and Its Principal Problems
United Nations Economic Commission for Latin America.

The founding document of structuralist development economics and dependency theory. Argues that the terms of trade systematically favor industrialized core countries over commodity-exporting periphery countries.
Cardoso, Fernando Henrique and Faletto, Enzo
Dependency and Development in Latin America
University of California Press. (Originally published in Spanish, 1969.)

The most sophisticated dependency theory text. It avoids mechanical determinism by examining how domestic class alliances mediate dependency relations. Influential in both IR and comparative politics.
States and the Reemergence of Global Finance: From Bretton Woods to the 1990s

Shows that financial globalization was a political choice, not a natural outgrowth of markets. States actively created the conditions for global capital mobility. Essential for understanding structural financial power.
A Technique for the Measurement of Attitudes
Archives of Psychology, no. 140.
The original description of the Likert summated-rating scale. The five-point format described here is the ancestor of the seven-point format used in this inventory.
The Nature of Belief Systems in Mass Publics
In D. E. Apter (ed.), Ideology and Discontent. Free Press.

The foundational text on constraint in political belief systems. Asks whether ordinary citizens hold coherent ideological positions, a question relevant to what self-report instruments like this one can and cannot measure.
The Nature and Origins of Mass Opinion

Argues that survey responses capture a running sample of considerations, not stable underlying attitudes. One of the strongest challenges to the idea that self-report instruments measure fixed preferences.
Expert Political Judgment: How Good Is It? How Can We Know?

A large-scale study of expert forecasting accuracy. The finding that fox-like analysts (who draw on many frameworks) outperform hedgehog-like ones (committed to a single theory) is directly relevant to how this inventory should be interpreted.
Sil, Rudra and Katzenstein, Peter J.
Beyond Paradigms: Analytic Eclecticism in the Study of World Politics
The case for drawing on multiple IR traditions rather than committing to one paradigm. Directly relevant to why this inventory treats the runner-up classification as important, not just the primary.

Continue reading: when outside scrutiny depends on the developer
Freedom to publish starts before publication

An evaluator can be free to publish criticism and still depend on the developer for the chance to investigate. In Larch's case, transferring admission authority changes who can get that chance. It does not change what an admitted team is allowed to do.

This is the project's judgment about the supplied arrangement. It supports examining admission rules alongside research and publication rights. It does not establish that Larch will use its veto to suppress criticism, or that any present-day institution does so.

The mechanism is selection. A right to publish applies to people who have already gained access. If an organization can exclude a qualified applicant, it can affect which questions get investigated without editing the eventual report. The fiction holds competence criteria, screening staff, budget and waiting times constant, so the replay supplies no extra workload or technical reason for moving that authority.

Seger and colleagues distinguish public release from controlled access for external evaluation. They discuss research interfaces with permissions suited to the work, and propose mediation of researcher admission to address favoritism and developer control over research opportunities. These are proposals and concerns in a 2023 report, not proof that a particular access program is independent or effective.

Only the enclave's admission authority changes
The three proposed release plans over the same three-month period. Every entry describes the exercise's fictional terms or identifies a term it leaves unspecified.

Research context: the cited report discusses structured access and independent mediation. It does not supply Larch's permissions. In particular, this exercise specifies an admission veto, not a new power to revoke access or block publication after admission.
The tradeoff survives the comparison

A release committee could accept developer admission control because it wants the organization responsible for hosting the model to retain authority over entry. That is a governance choice with a cost: outside scrutiny can depend on the subject's permission. The exercise does not establish that the independent panel has better judgment, that the veto will be abused, or that public release is safe.

Public weights avoid this admission gate, but the supplied terms also remove Larch's ability to recall downloaded copies. Hosted access retains the model inside the institute while denying outsiders direct examination of its internals. Neither alternative becomes consequence-free because the enclave has a governance weakness. Choosing one requires saying which cost you are prepared to accept.
What would change the judgment?

A binding appeal that can overturn an exclusion would weaken the claim that developer permission is decisive. Evidence of how qualified applicants are admitted or rejected, whether research permissions fit the questions being asked, and whether critical findings can be published would matter more than the label “external.” These are questions for evaluating a real arrangement; the exercise supplies none of those records.

For discussion, take one disputed application and ask who could reverse a refusal. Then ask which new cost that safeguard would impose. That keeps the debate on an institutional choice people can examine, while leaving open whether any particular release plan is justified.

An AI offers a life beyond Earth.
What would make it an offer you could accept?

An artificial superintelligence has helped develop treatments for diseases that resisted human medicine and technologies capable of greatly reducing material scarcity. In this story, those achievements are given. How people use them remains contested.

Now it announces that it will leave Earth. It offers settlements elsewhere for anyone who wants to accompany it. Those who stay keep the tools already shared and govern themselves. Declining does not cost them access.
The AI says it will neither govern Earth nor punish refusal. It warns that a future superintelligence built on Earth could be dangerous. What power it reserves over such a system has not been agreed.
You are considering the invitation. Someone close to you intends to stay. You do not know whether you could meet again, or who could enforce a right to return.

Consider a fictional adult deciding whether to leave. Other people in their life will stay. A policy assessment must consider separation, return and authority without requiring you to imagine your own relationships.
The AI’s achievements show formidable competence. They do not establish every claim about life beyond Earth.

Departure does not settle jurisdiction
Travel and settlement are offered. Earth keeps self-government and access to the tools. Return, future reunion and reliable communication have no agreed terms. The AI’s successor policy remains open.

The revised offer promises a return service, maintained for each traveler’s lifetime; two-way communication, subject to travel-related delays; and departure from the settlement without asking the AI’s permission.

Earth keeps the same tools and self-government. The offer still supplies no independently verified travel time, enforcement mechanism, or guarantee of reunion with a particular person. The successor policy is still open.

The AI has left. Earth still governs itself and retains the tools. Consider three possible arrangements for successor AI, then separately decide what information and intervention powers you would authorize. A vote for one does not silently grant the others.

/decisions/who-gets-access

The fictional Larch Research Institute must decide how to provide access to a capable model for the next three months. Its internal tests show useful software and cyber assistance but do not establish autonomous attacks, and no misuse has been observed outside testing.
Publish downloadable weights that anyone can run or modify. Released copies cannot be recalled.
Admit qualified external evaluators to a secure enclave, with general access through a monitored hosted service.
Offer a monitored, rate-limited hosted service, keeping weights and deeper evaluation inside Larch.
An independent panel admits qualified teams and makes final admission decisions. Larch cannot veto a qualified applicant.
The revised arrangement gives Larch final admission power and a veto over applicants who meet the same criteria.

Staffing, budget, screening criteria, wait times, research permissions and publication rights stay the same. Capability and misuse evidence, and the public-weights and hosted-service options, also stay fixed.
Qualified enclave participants may inspect and modify the model, export approved findings and publish criticism under the existing export terms. Weights remain inside the enclave.
Larch does not know how much new benefit or misuse wider access would produce. No arrangement guarantees safety or useful criticism.

Publishing the weights would let anyone run or modify the model, and Larch could not retrieve the released copies. An enclave gives qualified outsiders access without distributing those weights. A precautionary argument favors keeping that control while further testing examines the cyber risks and what would justify wider release.
Who else gains access?

Publishing weights would let competitors build on Larch's work. Hosted access or an enclave would keep the weights inside, while offering different opportunities for outsiders to investigate. A strategic argument asks which researchers should gain access, what they could learn, and how that knowledge might benefit a rival.

Other institutes could use comparable admission criteria and recognize one another's evaluations. The independent panel gives Larch less discretion to exclude qualified applicants. A coordination argument asks whether that arrangement could support cooperation between institutes, and how a developer veto would affect their willingness to rely on it.
Who can be held to account?

Evaluators may publish criticism under both arrangements. The difference is who gets inside: an independent panel admits qualified teams in the first; Larch can veto them in the second. Public accountability raises another question: who appoints that decision-maker, oversees its choices and hears a complaint from an excluded researcher?

The enclave requires people to screen applicants and support their work. A state-capacity argument asks whether the responsible bodies have the staff, money and authority to do that job. Before choosing, it would need to know how much work each arrangement requires and who can deliver it.
Who is left outside the qualified group?

Publishing the weights lets researchers outside the qualified group reproduce and modify the model. An independent admission panel still leaves some researchers out. Wider access would reduce that dependence on permission, but Larch would lose the ability to recall the copies. Is access for more researchers worth giving up that control?
Outside evaluators test for dangerous capability before release. Release is staged and gated on those tests.

They disagree about what the check answers to. The Steward binds it to the capability itself: cross a threshold and the burden of proof rises, whoever is in charge. The Guardrailist binds it to public oversight: a check the public cannot contest is a private arrangement, however cautious.
Both treat AI governance as a problem for states, and both distrust rules that exist only on paper.

The Competitor asks what keeps a capability edge under rivalry and reads institutions as instruments of that contest. The Capacity Builder asks who can supervise, procure, and verify in practice, and what an edge is worth to a state that depends on the firms it is supposed to govern.
Both worry that frontier capability is concentrating in a few labs and a few states.

The Ecosystem Builder answers with access: put models and tools in more hands, so no gatekeeper decides what can be studied or built. The Architect answers with rules: cross-border standards and verification that outlast any one lab's advantage. Each sees a cost in the other's cure. Wider access allows more researchers to reproduce the work, while Larch loses the ability to recall released copies. Shared rules raise a different concern: whether the participating firms and states would exclude others.
Both want enforceable rules and distrust voluntary self-governance by labs.

The Architect looks outward: legitimacy comes from standards and verification that rival states accept. The Guardrailist looks inward: legitimacy comes from domestic institutions the public can hold to account. They may back the same rule for a model. They part over what makes it legitimate, a standard agreed among states or a decision a domestic public can contest.

The challenge of building AI systems that reliably pursue goals matching human values and intentions. An aligned model does what its designers and users actually want, even in novel situations. Alignment is difficult because specifying human goals precisely enough to prevent unintended behavior at scale is an unsolved problem.

A defined level of AI capability that triggers additional governance responses, such as mandatory evaluation, restricted deployment, or escalation to a regulatory body. Thresholds can be specified by benchmark performance, by particular dangerous capabilities such as autonomous cyberattack, or by the volume of compute used in training.

Policy approaches that regulate access to the hardware used to train and run large AI models, including GPUs, TPUs, and the data centers that house them. Because advanced chips are produced by a small number of firms in limited locations, compute is treated as a potentially tractable chokepoint for governance. Proposals range from export controls to know-your-customer requirements on cloud providers.

How quickly an AI system moves from research or limited testing into widespread real-world use. Arguments for faster deployment emphasize social benefits and real-world learning. Arguments for slower deployment emphasize the need for evaluations and safeguards to catch up before exposure reaches scale.

AI capabilities that have both civilian and military or harmful applications. A model that accelerates biological research may also lower barriers to bioweapon design. Dual-use concerns complicate openness decisions: wide release may generate broad social value while also enabling misuse that is difficult to reverse.

Structured testing of AI systems for specific capabilities, safety properties, or risks, run by labs internally, by independent third parties, or by government agencies. Evaluations are the primary mechanism for detecting dangerous capabilities before deployment, but current methods have significant gaps, particularly for emergent or deceptive behaviors.

A large AI system at or near the current limit of capability, typically trained using massive compute, data, and human feedback. The term refers to the leading edge of what is technically possible rather than a fixed capability level. Frontier governance decisions may need to anticipate capabilities that do not yet exist in deployed systems.

Research and methods aimed at understanding what an AI model has learned and why it produces particular outputs. At its strongest, interpretability would let auditors verify a model's internal representations and goals rather than relying on behavioral tests alone. Current interpretability tools remain limited for frontier systems.

The numerical parameters learned during training that define an AI model's behavior. Releasing model weights allows anyone to run, fine-tune, or modify the model without the original developer's infrastructure. Open-weight release differs from open-source code: it shares the trained artifact, not just the training procedure.

Whether AI model weights, training code, or data are made publicly accessible rather than kept proprietary or gated behind an API. Proponents argue openness enables broader innovation, reduces incumbency concentration, and allows independent safety research. Critics argue it makes dangerous capabilities difficult to contain once released.

A country's or institution's capacity to govern, develop, or constrain AI within its jurisdiction, independent of foreign providers. Sovereignty concerns arise when critical AI infrastructure, including compute, models, and data, is controlled by foreign entities or a small number of private firms. Policy responses include domestic compute investment, local data requirements, and limits on foreign AI procurement.

Technical or institutional methods for confirming that AI systems or governance commitments meet stated requirements. In arms-control contexts, verification involves inspection or monitoring that allows external parties to check compliance. AI verification is technically underdeveloped: it is currently difficult to verify what a model can do, what data it was trained on, or whether safety commitments have been honored.

Managing AI Risks in an Era of Rapid Progress

Emily M. Bender, Timnit Gebru, Angelina McMillan-Major, Shmargaret Shmitchell

The most influential articulation of present-harms-first concerns: environmental cost, data ethics, documentation gaps, and risks of systems deployed before their harms are understood. Counterpoint to capability-first governance.
The Malicious Use of Artificial Intelligence: Forecasting, Prevention, and Mitigation
Miles Brundage et al.

Forecasts how AI capabilities could be misused across cyber, physical, and political domains. A useful threat-model primer that applies regardless of where you stand on deployment pace or oversight structures.
Human Compatible: Artificial Intelligence and the Problem of Control

The technical and philosophical case for why advanced AI requires fundamentally different design principles: corrigibility, uncertainty about human preferences, and the ability to be corrected. Argues control is not a secondary concern.
An Overview of Catastrophic AI Risks
Dan Hendrycks, Mantas Mazeika, Thomas Woodside

A systematic survey of AI risk categories, including misuse, misalignment, and structural risks, that argues precautionary governance is warranted even under deep uncertainty. A reference for the frontier-risk case.
The Precipice: Existential Risk and the Future of Humanity
Situates AI risk in the broader context of catastrophic and existential risk. Explains why severe low-probability scenarios can justify urgent governance under uncertainty.
Final Report: National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence
Eric Schmidt, Robert Work et al. (NSCAI)

The U.S. government's most comprehensive assessment of AI and national security. Argues competition with China is a structural feature of the AI era and that democratic governments must maintain capability leadership.
Battlefield Singularity: Artificial Intelligence, Military Revolution, and China's Future Military Power
Elsa Kania (Center for a New American Security)

Early influential analysis of China's military AI strategy. Argues that AI will reshape military competition and that capability gaps compound over time. Shaped subsequent U.S. strategic thinking on the domain.
Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead

A provocation arguing that AGI timelines are short, that strategic competition will intensify as capabilities grow, and that leading democracies must treat frontier AI as a matter of national security.
Should Artificial Intelligence Governance Be Centralised?
Peter Cihon, Matthijs Maas, Luke Kemp

Analyzes the case for centralized versus polycentric AI governance. Finds benefits to centralization for managing concentrated risks but warns of fragility and institutional capture. Useful for thinking through the institutional-design tradeoffs.
Rules for a Flat World: Why Humans Invented Law and How to Reinvent It for a Complex Global Economy

Makes the case for adaptive, distributed, and privately supplied legal infrastructure. Relevant to AI governance debates about whether traditional state-based regulatory institutions are the right vehicle for fast-moving technology.
Toward Trustworthy AI Development: Mechanisms for Supporting Verifiable Claims
Miles Brundage et al.

Proposes technical and institutional mechanisms, including audit, certification, and red-teaming, that would let coordination commitments become credible rather than merely declaratory. A constructive complement to coordination-optimism.
Atlas of AI: Power, Politics, and the Planetary Costs of Artificial Intelligence

Maps AI as a material and political infrastructure. Argues that governance must address power asymmetries between developers and affected communities, not only technical safety. Required reading for accountability-first positions.
Closing the AI Accountability Gap: Defining an End-to-End Framework for Internal Algorithmic Auditing
Inioluwa Deborah Raji et al.

Proposes internal audit frameworks for AI systems that foreground social harm rather than only technical performance. Influential for accountability-first governance approaches that want mechanisms, not just principles.
AI Now Report 2023

Annual survey of AI's social and political implications. Argues for public regulation, worker protections, and civil society oversight. Represents the democratic-accountability wing of the governance debate.
The Long Game: China's Grand Strategy to Displace American Order

Reconstructs China's strategy across economic, military, and political domains. Shows how state capacity, alongside intent, determines whether governance commitments can be credibly made and enforced.
Strengthening and Democratizing the U.S. Artificial Intelligence Innovation Ecosystem
Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET)

Policy analysis of gaps in U.S. AI procurement, workforce, and regulatory capacity. Identifies implementation capacity as the critical bottleneck: technical staff, institutional knowledge, and agency competence.
Government by Algorithm: Artificial Intelligence in Federal Administrative Agencies
David Freeman Engstrom et al.

Surveys how federal agencies already use AI and finds that capacity gaps are the primary barrier to accountable algorithmic governance, rather than a lack of rules. Grounds the state-capacity argument in current administrative practice.
Release Strategies and the Social Impacts of Language Models
Irene Solaiman et al.
Evaluates open, staged, and closed release postures and their social tradeoffs. An early systematic treatment of openness as a governance variable rather than a binary choice.
On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models
Rishi Bommasani et al. (Stanford CRFM)

Comprehensive survey of large foundation models documenting both the broad benefits of accessible general-purpose AI and the governance challenges concentration creates. Grounds the open-ecosystem case in empirical analysis.
Building Open-Source AI

Makes the case that open-source AI development produces better safety properties through distributed scrutiny, rather than worse ones. Argues for openness as a positive safety strategy rather than a concession to speed.
A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence

Argues that current deep learning architectures do not lead to the kind of agency or strategic autonomy that catastrophic-risk scenarios require. Challenges the technical premises of frontier-risk governance from inside the field.
Rebooting AI: Building Artificial Intelligence We Can Trust
Gary Marcus, Ernest Davis

Argues that current AI capabilities are substantially overstated and that governance organized around catastrophic frontier risk may be addressing the wrong problem. Useful for stress-testing precautionary assumptions.
When Speed Kills: Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems and the Dangers of Rushing to Weaponize AI

Argues that competitive dynamics in military AI create pressure to deploy systems before they are ready, increasing catastrophic failure risk. Challenges the assumption that competitive urgency improves national security outcomes.
Towards a Global AI Governance Architecture
Samir Saran, Akhil Deo (Observer Research Foundation)

Argues that governance built on U.S.-China competition will fail to include the Global South and will undermine long-term legitimacy. Challenges competition-first governance as insufficient for durable global stability.
The Tragedy of Great Power Politics

The foundational text for offensive realism. Argues that international institutions are largely epiphenomenal and that major powers will defect from cooperative arrangements when vital interests conflict. The sharpest test of coordination-optimism.
The Long Game: China's Grand Strategy to Displace American Order

Read as a critique: documents how China uses multilateral institutions strategically to advance competitive goals rather than build durable cooperation. Challenges the assumption that coordination frameworks will bind leading powers symmetrically.
Incompleteness: A Regulatory Design Challenge for AI

Argues that traditional democratic regulatory institutions, including legislation, agencies, and courts, are structurally poorly suited to the speed and complexity of AI. Challenges the assumption that more democratic accountability automatically yields better governance.
Regulating by Robot: Administrative Decision Making in the Machine-Learning Era
Cary Coglianese, David Lehr

Analyzes when algorithmic decision-making can be compatible with existing legal accountability standards and when it challenges them. Pushes back on blanket democratic-oversight arguments by showing where they apply and where they don't.

Argues that AI's economic and political harms are partly enabled by excessive state subsidies and incumbency protection for large AI developers. Challenges state-capacity arguments by questioning whether more government investment in AI is straightforwardly beneficial.
The Values Encoded in Machine Learning Research
Abeba Birhane et al.

Finds that institutional actors deploying AI systems tend to encode narrow performance and efficiency values over equity. Challenges state-capacity arguments by asking: capacity to do what, in whose interest?
Open-Sourcing Highly Capable Foundation Models
Elizabeth Seger et al. (Centre for the Governance of AI)

A detailed assessment concluding that for highly capable models, open-weights release shifts risk substantially and that openness objectives can often be achieved through less risky mechanisms. The most systematic case against unrestricted open release.
Open (for Business): Big Tech, Concentrated Power, and the Political Economy of Open AI
David Gray Widder, Sarah West, Meredith Whittaker

A critical analysis distinguishing genuine openness from strategic use of open-source framing by incumbents. Argues that openness alone does not address concentration and may entrench it under some conditions.
Governing Artificial Intelligence in China and the United States
Huw Roberts et al.

Compares Chinese and U.S. approaches to AI governance, finding more convergence on high-level principles than is commonly assumed but significant divergence on implementation, rights, and surveillance. An antidote to pure competition framing.
Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence

The first global normative framework on AI ethics, adopted by 193 member states. Establishes human rights, dignity, and environmental sustainability as governance anchors. Represents the multilateral rather than great-power governance vision.
The Costs of Connection: How Data Is Colonizing Human Life
Nick Couldry, Ulises A. Mejias

Argues that the data economy replicates colonial extraction patterns. Relevant for Global South AI governance: questions whether current frameworks address the asymmetric costs borne by countries outside the frontier.
Artificial Intelligence Policy: A Primer and Roadmap

A foundational legal overview of the AI policy space that identifies challenges no single national framework can solve alone. Sets up the case for why governance must operate at multiple jurisdictional levels.

This pattern is slow to crown one explanation. Faced with a case, it asks what rivalry explains, what rules explain, and what legitimacy explains, and it waits for the evidence to separate them before it treats a single school as the default.

If an exposed ally asks for troops on its border, this pattern separates into two paths. One weighs coalition strain and escalation risk and favors restraint; the other reads the request as a test of commitment and hardens around deterrence. Which path it takes depends on which cost the case makes visible first.

If a ministry must choose between a cheap foreign digital stack and a costlier allied one, this pattern stops hedging. Dependence on a rival's infrastructure is the kind of fact that makes it choose control over open exchange.

It is easy to mistake for Coalitions First, because both resist maximalism, and for Different by Domain, because both can look unsettled. On deterrence, this approach supports clear limits on escalation. Where a country depends on one supplier or route, it is more willing to use controls.

This realist pattern treats competition as lasting and treats every contest as a place where a state can overreach. Its first move is to hold position without taking on commitments that are expensive to keep or hard to reverse.
Given a rival probing the boundary, this pattern backs deterrence and a ceiling together: hold the line, name the limit, and watch for the escalation trap.
Security competition is the starting point for reading most major-power cases.
Restraint here is a way to protect position and avoid strategic drift, and no sign of softness.
Order and precedent carry more weight than expansive moral ambition.
Openings where sustained pressure would improve the strategic balance.

If a NATO ministerial is choosing an eastern-flank posture, this pattern favors reinforcement, visible resolve, and a stated ceiling. It reads open-ended escalation as the risk to plan against, so it prefers a posture allies can hold for years to one that signals most in the first month.

If a supplier that is also a rival controls a chokepoint, this pattern supports targeted export controls and protection of the chokepoint. It applies the same test it applies to force: is the control worth the dependence it creates elsewhere, and can it be held?

It is easy to mistake for Power and Leverage, because both start from rivalry, and for Coalitions First, because both accept limits. The difference: this pattern treats the strategic ceiling as the first question, and Power and Leverage treats it as a later correction.

Leverage is there to be used

On deterrence, this pattern strengthens visible pressure. On chokepoints and dependence, it supports control over them.

This pattern sees competition as the ground condition of major-power politics. Where the constraint-first version looks for the ceiling, this one tests openings, raises costs for the rival, and converts advantage into position while it can.

Security competition is the strongest explanatory signal in the pattern.

No authority stands above states, so power and self-help decide more than rules or good intentions.

Realism starts from a blunt fact: there is no government above governments. Nobody can reliably punish a state that cheats or protect a state that is attacked. So states look after themselves. Structural realists put the whole argument on that fact. Classical realists add a second one, a drive for power in human nature that statecraft has to manage. Both conclude that even a state that wants peace cannot be sure its neighbors do, and prepares for the worst. From that premise realists expect recurring patterns: arms races, balancing coalitions, and competition between states that would each prefer to cooperate. The security dilemma is the tragic version. Weapons bought for defense look like preparation for attack from across the border, and the reply looks the same from the other side. Nobody wanted the spiral, and nobody can safely step out of it. Realism is a family of arguments, and the family quarrels. Offensive realists hold that anarchy pushes great powers to seek as much power as they can, because there is no safe point to stop. Defensive realists reply that the system often rewards restraint and punishes expansion. What the family shares is the claim that power and self-help are permanent features of world politics, and that better institutions or warmer feelings will not remove them.
Anarchy, the absence of a central authority above states, is the condition everything else follows from.
Because states cannot be sure of one another's intentions, each must provide for its own security.
The distribution of power among states, whether one leads or several compete, shapes conflict and cooperation more than any other factor.
Relative gains matter. A deal that strengthens a rival more than it strengthens you weakens your position over time.
Defensive measures look threatening from outside. The security dilemma produces arms spirals that no party intended.

Morgenthau and Niebuhr ground the argument in a human drive for power, with the structure of the system as a second factor. The tradition concerns itself with statecraft, the judgment of leaders, and the tragic character of politics among nations.

Waltz moves the explanation from human nature to the shape of the system: anarchy plus the distribution of capabilities. Leaders matter less. The structure rewards some behavior and punishes the rest, whoever is in office.

Mearsheimer argues that anarchy pushes great powers to maximize their power, because a state can never know how much security is enough. The safest position is to be the strongest, so competition never settles.

Glaser, Van Evera, and Snyder argue that the system often rewards restraint. Most wars come from miscalculation, domestic pathologies, or spirals that both sides could have avoided. Anarchy by itself does not require endless expansion.
