Whether labs should have to present a more explicit argument for why deployment is justified before higher-stakes use.
This is not asking whether every useful model needs the same level of review.

Advanced models should enter critical infrastructure through staged real-world deployment, because operational learning improves assurance faster than waiting for comprehensive pre-deployment guarantees.
Whether bounded operational use is a better route to assurance than waiting for comprehensive evidence in advance.
It still assumes bounded pilots, operational monitoring, and a practiced rollback path.
Frontier labs should face mandatory reporting of serious safety or security incidents, including near misses that reveal dangerous failure modes.
Whether incident reporting should be a public-governance requirement rather than a discretionary internal practice.
This is not asking whether every minor product bug belongs in a national reporting regime.
Frontier labs should retain primary responsibility for auditing their safety and security controls, because internal teams can adapt scrutiny faster than recurring external reviews.
Whether resident technical teams are better placed than recurring outside auditors to provide continuous assurance.
It still leaves public authorities responsible for setting enforceable duties and acting on serious failures.
Broad access to high-capability model weights can distribute scrutiny and innovation beyond a few frontier labs, making openness a governance asset alongside security controls.
Whether widening access can improve independent scrutiny, competition, and the distribution of technical capability.
It still accepts tighter controls when a release creates specific, severe, and hard-to-reverse risks.
Frontier governance gains legitimacy from demonstrated technical competence and effective safeguards, even when agenda-setting remains concentrated among leading labs and major powers.
Whether competent performance can confer legitimacy despite concentrated control over priorities.
It treats representation as one source of legitimacy alongside competence and performance.
Future AI systems with credible experiences or interests should receive moral consideration alongside humans, even when that shifts governance away from human-centered priorities.
Whether credible evidence of machine experience should widen the moral community beyond humans.
It leaves the moral status of current systems open and addresses a future threshold.
Radical AI-enabled human enhancement should face stronger public limits unless its benefits, risks, and access are politically shared rather than privately captured.
Whether governance should treat extreme augmentation as a political and distributive question, not only as a private consumer choice.
This is not asking whether all medical or assistive enhancement is suspect.
A leading lab says a new model may have crossed an internal threshold for dangerous cyber capability. What should happen first?
A frontier developer privately reports a plausible threshold crossing for dangerous cyber capability. Which first move is most justified?
A capability threshold is a defined level of AI capability that triggers additional governance responses. Outside evaluation means assessment by independent experts or regulators, not the lab itself.
Treat the threshold crossing as a stop signal and pause broader release until outsiders test it.
Treat it as a containment problem: keep it in tightly controlled channels while gathering more evidence under supervision.
Continue limited deployment and internal mitigation because delay can also create real strategic and social costs.
Make threshold crossing a formal tripwire: require outside evaluation before further scale-up.
Treat it as a containment-and-reporting event: no broad release, but continue tightly controlled testing with government visibility.
Treat strategic delay as too costly and keep pushing forward while managing risk inside the lab.
Reduce unilateral lab discretion by widening qualified outside scrutiny, even if control becomes looser.
A credible rumor suggests a rival great power may be close to a frontier breakthrough. What should your government prioritize?
Verification means confirming whether the report is accurate before acting on it. Crisis communication channels are diplomatic pathways that reduce the risk of miscalculation or escalation.
Stabilize first: open crisis channels and verify the report before shifting posture.
Quietly hedge: harden allied defenses, monitoring, and readiness without treating the rumor as settled fact.
Assume the warning is real and accelerate for advantage before the window closes.
Build verification and confidence-building channels first, even if it slows immediate mobilization.
Quietly mobilize allied defenses and monitoring while avoiding a public escalatory spiral.
Treat the rumor as an early-warning signal and accelerate aggressively.
Use the shock to press for a plurilateral restraint arrangement with verification hooks, even at short-term cost.
When frontier models become more capable, which release approach seems best?

Model weights are the learned parameters that define a model's behavior. Releasing weights lets anyone run or modify the model. An API keeps the model centrally controlled but allows external use under terms set by the developer.
Capability containment: keep weights closed and access tightly gated as systems become more capable.
Instrumented access: allow monitored API or sandbox use so outside testing continues without general release.
Plural diffusion: widen access to prevent a few firms or states from becoming permanent gatekeepers.
Closed release with hard gatekeeping for weights and frontier access.
Instrumented API access with staged evaluations, monitoring, and revocation triggers.
Qualified wider release so more actors can inspect, build, and avoid dependence on a few labs.
Public release as the standing default unless a narrow, concrete risk case overrides it.
How should frontier AI be used in national defense?
Bounded defense use means tightly scoped applications — like logistics or information triage — where human authority over final decisions is preserved and the mission set is clearly restricted.
Keep frontier AI largely outside defense planning so militaries do not normalize dependence too early.
Use it only for bounded decision support, not broader operational integration, and keep humans in real authority.
Integrate it deeply because strategic competition will not wait for cleaner norms.
Adopt strong restraint: slow uptake, narrow mission sets, and avoid building doctrine around frontier AI.
Permit bounded decision support and limited operations only where human authority remains real and auditable.
Fold frontier AI deeply into competition, planning, and military advantage.
Freeze further integration until stronger international norms or reciprocal limits emerge.
If countries try to coordinate on frontier AI safeguards, what matters most?
Verification in AI governance means technical or institutional methods that let outside parties confirm whether commitments are being honored, rather than relying on self-reporting alone.
Credibility first: a narrower deal with real verification beats a broad promise nobody can check.
Participation first: start with lighter commitments major powers will actually sign, then harden later.
Self-reliance first: build domestic enforcement capacity because paper agreements will not carry enough weight.
Verification-first arrangements, even if the initial coalition is narrow.
Broad but lighter-touch coordination that can attract more parties and deepen later.
National enforcement capacity first; external coordination should stay secondary.
Club governance among frontier-capable actors first, with wider expansion only after rules stabilize.
If AI becomes much more capable, what should governance protect most strongly?

People disagree about this question partly because they have different views on how much current human institutions should constrain future development, and partly because they weight different kinds of risks differently.
Human authority and the ability to slow or reverse systems that begin to outrun governance.
Fair distribution of gains and protection against domination by firms, states, or technical elites.
Room for large civilizational upside even if institutions have to adapt under strain.
Preserve strong human authority and real reversibility.
Build institutions that distribute gains and reduce domination, dependency, or capture.
Accept more transformational pathways if the upside is large and governance can stay credible under strain.
Treat human and possibly broader sentient flourishing as the key moral lens, even if older institutions strain.

A frontier lab has 24 hours to report a serious internal incident. The system never affected the public, yet testing revealed a dangerous failure mode. What reporting and redeployment rules should regulators require?
A safety case is a structured argument for why deployment is justified in a given context. A near miss is an incident that reveals a dangerous failure mode even if major harm did not occur this time.
Create a public trigger: mandatory reporting, outside review, and no broader deployment until the failure mode is understood.
Contain and learn: keep the system in a narrow supervised channel while government sees the incident and fixes are tested.
Treat it mainly as an internal lab-governance failure unless a broader pattern emerges.
Raise the bar structurally: no higher-risk redeployment without a safety case, audit, and public incident summary.
Make this a formal reporting trigger: mandatory disclosure, outside review, and a pause until the failure mode is understood.
Contain and monitor: keep it in a narrow supervised channel while government is notified and controls are tightened.
Treat it as a lab-governance matter first and avoid turning one event into a standing public trigger.
Require a structured safety case, external audit, and incident-disclosure summary before scaling resumes.
A coalition of major compute providers proposes licensing extreme-scale training runs and imposing stricter weight-security obligations. What posture seems best?

Compute governance uses the hardware and cloud infrastructure needed for frontier training as a governance chokepoint. Weight security means preventing theft or uncontrolled release of the model parameters themselves.
Use compute as the choke point: license extreme-scale training and harden weight security now.
Use compute controls only if they are temporary, reviewable, and checked against cartel abuse.
Reject concentrated compute gatekeeping because it entrenches hierarchy before proving its safety value.
Build allied compute controls to deny adversarial access even if governance becomes openly club-like.
Treat compute licensing and stronger weight security as the most workable near-term frontier lever.
Use compute controls only with anti-cartel safeguards, outside review, and regular sunset tests.
Reject concentrated compute gatekeeping because it hardens hierarchy before proving its safety value.
Build club-style compute controls among trusted states first and treat broader legitimacy as a later problem.
A government wants to authorize frontier models for grid balancing, telecom recovery, and emergency coordination. What should matter most before approval?

Critical infrastructure refers to systems whose failure would create large public harms. Rollback means being able to remove or disable an AI system quickly if it begins to fail or behave unpredictably.
Treat critical infrastructure as a high-assurance zone and do not approve until rollback and fail-safe regimes are much stronger.
Permit only narrow pilots where humans can intervene, incidents must be reported, and outside auditors can stop expansion.
Approve sooner because resilience gains from deployment outweigh the risks of delay.
Require a governance structure with public legitimacy before a few providers become infrastructural gatekeepers.
Treat critical infrastructure as a high-assurance zone and block approval until stronger rollback and assurance regimes exist.
Permit narrow public pilots only where humans can intervene, external auditors can halt expansion, and incidents must be reported.
Approve sooner because resilience gains matter enough to justify moving before ideal assurance exists.
Require a governance structure with stronger public legitimacy before a few providers become infrastructural gatekeepers.
Major-power peace remains fragile when the balance of power is shifting.
Does a shift in power make a peaceful relationship harder to maintain?
How military, economic, and strategic capability is distributed among the strongest states.
Even without a world government, shared rules can make cooperation last.
Can shared rules help states cooperate when no higher authority can enforce them?
The United States should take all steps including the use of force to prevent aggression by any expansionist power
Kertzer et al. (2014), Moral Support: How Moral Values Shape Foreign Policy Attitudes, supplementary appendix §1.1, p. 2, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022381614000073
A new governing coalition often redirects foreign policy even when the external threat remains unchanged.
Can elections, leadership changes, and domestic coalitions shift foreign policy as much as events abroad?
The meaning of a military buildup depends more on the states' history and mutual trust than on the size of the force.
When states judge a military move, do past relations and trust tell us more than the size of the force?
The United States needs to cooperate more with the United Nations.
Kertzer et al. (2014), Moral Support: How Moral Values Shape Foreign Policy Attitudes, supplementary appendix §1.1, p. 2, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022381614000073
In a crisis, control over credit, production, and supply-chain chokepoints shapes state choices more than military capability alone.
Do finance and supply-chain dependence constrain states more than military differences do?
When a state keeps pushing for gains beyond what it needs for defense, rivals and bystanders often respond in ways that leave it less secure.
Does seeking gains beyond defense usually trigger resistance and leave a state less secure?
The U.S. should mind its own business internationally and let other countries get along the best they can on their own.
Kertzer et al. (2014), Moral Support: How Moral Values Shape Foreign Policy Attitudes, supplementary appendix §1.1, pp. 2–3, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022381614000073
A stable international order is often worth preserving even when serious injustice remains unresolved.
When stability and justice conflict, should preserving order usually come first?
What most often keeps alliances together under real pressure?
Choose the explanation you would use first.
Alliances hold when members believe the leading power can and will bear the cost of defense.
Planning structures, standing commitments, and repeated coordination make alliance promises more credible.
Alliances endure when domestic coalitions, budgets, and public tolerance can sustain them over time.
Alliances hold when they are seen as legitimate and identity-consistent, not only as efficient bargains.
Rather than simply countering our opponents’ thrusts, it is necessary to strike at the heart of an opponent’s power.
Kertzer et al. (2014), Moral Support: How Moral Values Shape Foreign Policy Attitudes, supplementary appendix §1.1, p. 2, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022381614000073
Uncertainty about another state's long-term intentions makes continued military preparation necessary even during sustained cooperation.
Does uncertainty about another state's future behavior push states to prepare for conflict?
It is essential for the United States to work with other nations to solve problems such as overpopulation, hunger, and pollution.
Kertzer et al. (2014), Moral Support: How Moral Values Shape Foreign Policy Attitudes, supplementary appendix §1.1, p. 2, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022381614000073
Monitoring and repeated contact can keep international agreements alive even when trust is thin.
Can monitoring and regular contact keep an agreement working when the parties do not trust each other?
We should not think so much in international terms but concentrate more on our own national problems.
Kertzer et al. (2014), Moral Support: How Moral Values Shape Foreign Policy Attitudes, supplementary appendix §1.1, pp. 2–3, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022381614000073
When economic interdependence becomes dangerous, what is usually the deeper problem?
Choose the cause, not a policy response.
Rivalry turns ties into leverage
Interdependence becomes dangerous mainly when strategic competition grows and states start treating economic exposure as a security risk.
Rules failed to keep up
The danger comes from weak guardrails. Better multilateral rules could preserve openness without so much coercive exposure.
The real weakness is political: domestic firms, regions, and interest groups become too embedded to adjust quickly when risk rises.
The structure was unequal
The vulnerability is built into who controls credit, production, and chokepoints. Exposure looks mutual until coercion begins.
States facing similar outside pressure can still act very differently because their internal politics differ.
Do different political systems and coalitions lead states facing the same pressure to respond differently?
American military strength is not the best way to ensure world peace.
Kertzer et al. (2014), Moral Support: How Moral Values Shape Foreign Policy Attitudes, supplementary appendix §1.1, p. 2, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022381614000073
A state's demand for recognition often changes which foreign-policy goals its leaders consider important.
Are a state's interests shaped partly by status, identity, and recognition?
Promoting and defending human rights in other countries is of utmost importance.
Kertzer et al. (2014), Moral Support: How Moral Values Shape Foreign Policy Attitudes, supplementary appendix §1.1, p. 2, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022381614000073
Economic rules often give stronger states lasting structural advantages that weaker states must work around.
Do global economic rules give some states built-in advantages over others?
A built-in benefit created by rules or institutions, not just a one-off bargaining win.
The U.S. needs to play an active role in solving conflicts around the world.
Kertzer et al. (2014), Moral Support: How Moral Values Shape Foreign Policy Attitudes, supplementary appendix §1.1, pp. 2–3, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022381614000073
Avoiding overextension is usually more important than pressing every opening for lasting advantage.
Is it usually safer to limit commitments than to take every chance for advantage?
The United States must demonstrate its resolve so that others do not take advantage of it.
Kertzer et al. (2014), Moral Support: How Moral Values Shape Foreign Policy Attitudes, supplementary appendix §1.1, p. 2, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022381614000073
When mass atrocities become severe enough, outside powers can justifiably override a state's sovereignty to stop them.
Can extreme harm to civilians justify military action without the government's consent?
This is about extreme emergency cases, not ordinary intervention or open-ended regime change.
The principle that a state normally controls what happens within its own territory.
Protecting the global environment is of utmost importance.
Kertzer et al. (2014), Moral Support: How Moral Values Shape Foreign Policy Attitudes, supplementary appendix §1.1, p. 2, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022381614000073
A rival is gaining ground. Which concern should come first?
If a durable strategic edge is available now, failing to use it will look reckless later.
The first danger is self-inflicted: excessive commitments and escalation can do more damage than a narrower rival gain.
Start with the home front
The real question is whether domestic coalitions, public tolerance, and fiscal capacity can carry the strategy at all.
Control the production base
Long-run advantage turns less on tactical posturing than on who controls technology, industry, and supply chains.
America’s conception of its leadership role in the world must be scaled down.
Kertzer et al. (2014), Moral Support: How Moral Values Shape Foreign Policy Attitudes, supplementary appendix §1.1, pp. 2–3, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022381614000073
A government is committing mass atrocities. Military action could save lives but weaken legal restraints on future interventions. What should govern the decision?
Which should guide the choice when law, civilian protection, authority, and likely outcomes point in different directions?
This is limited to severe mass atrocities, not ordinary disputes or open-ended regime change.
A limited and publicly stated authorization that defines what an intervention is allowed to do.
If the barrier against intervention erodes too easily, later abuses will do wider damage than this case can justify.
When civilian harm crosses an extreme threshold, the moral case can outweigh the usual presumption against intervention.
The decisive issue is whether a narrow, legitimate mandate exists. Emergency action is strongest when it is bounded and collectively framed.
Judge the likely outcome
The first test is whether action will plausibly protect people rather than widen the war or create a larger disaster.
A rival is catching up in advanced semiconductors while your firms depend on its supply chain. What should guide the response?
Choose the main goal of the response.
Preserve the strategic edge
Restrict broadly now. Closing the capability gap is itself the threat, and trade costs are secondary to preserving advantage.
The deeper contest is over production chokepoints and dependence. Build domestic capacity and unwind one-sided exposure.
Limit only the highest-risk technologies and do it with allies. Broad unilateral controls fracture the order you still need.
Treating every technological gap as a security emergency hardens rivalry and narrows room for future cooperation.
Mass killing is underway. A Security Council veto blocks UN authorization, but a regional body backs limited action. What should guide the response?
Choose the principle that should guide the response.
Which should carry most weight: UN authorization, stopping the killing, regional backing, or the risk of making things worse?
Regional backing is not the same as UN authorization.
Formal approval through an institution such as the UN Security Council.
Action without Security Council authorization weakens the legal framework that protects weaker states in harder cases to come.
Extreme human harm can override the normal procedural objection. The scale of the abuse changes the rule of thumb.
Regional backing plus a tightly limited mandate can justify emergency action without turning it into a general license.
The first question is whether outside action would likely protect civilians rather than widen the war and leave a worse political vacuum.
Major powers can build durable peace when each side accepts limits on military advantage.
Can mutual limits on military advantage make peace between major powers durable?
A rival's sustained restraint can provide credible evidence that its peaceful intentions will last.
Can sustained restraint reveal that a rival's peaceful intentions are likely to last?
Deep regional cooperation can make armed conflict among member states politically unthinkable.
Can deep regional cooperation make members expect disputes to remain peaceful?
International agreements endure when participating states retain enough power to enforce the bargain.
Do agreements last because participating states retain the power to uphold and enforce them?
States facing the same external threat usually adopt similar policies despite different political systems.
Do similar external threats push states toward similar policies across different political systems?
Regime change rarely alters a state's basic interests when its external position stays constant.
Do a state's basic interests survive regime change when its external position remains stable?
States define their interests mainly through security needs, resources, and geographic position.
Are state interests defined mainly by security needs, resources, and geography?
Recognition from other states rarely changes what governments seek in major security disputes.
Does recognition from other states have little effect on what governments seek in major security disputes?
Open markets usually give states enough flexibility to replace suppliers and absorb economic pressure.
Can open markets help states replace suppliers and withstand economic pressure?
Preventing a hostile power from dominating a key region can justify long-term commitments far from home.
Can blocking regional domination justify sustained commitments far from home?
Sustained forward presence gives allies confidence and denies rivals room to test regional limits.
Does forward presence reassure allies and reduce opportunities for rivals to test regional limits?
International courts should pursue grave crimes even when prosecutions complicate peace negotiations.
Should courts pursue grave crimes when prosecution could complicate peace negotiations?
Long stretches of peace among major powers usually depend on conditions that can weaken or disappear.
Does peace last only while the conditions supporting it remain in place?
Many international institutions mostly reflect what powerful states already want.
Do international institutions shape behavior on their own, or mainly reflect what powerful states want?
For most international crises, who controls credit, production, or market access is secondary to the immediate security and diplomatic facts.
In a fast-moving crisis, do security and diplomacy usually explain more than economic dependence?
There should usually be a strong default rule against outside intervention in another state's internal affairs.
Should non-intervention be the usual rule, including in morally difficult cases?
The principle that outside states should usually not use force or coercion inside another state's territory.
When what states say and what they deploy point in different directions, deployments are usually the safer guide.
When words and military deployments conflict, which is more reliable?
How a rival responds to being excluded from talks, denied diplomatic recognition, or treated as a lesser power can help predict what it will do next.
Can a rival's response to a perceived status slight help predict its next move?
The standing and recognition a state believes it deserves from other states.
Control over technology rules and critical infrastructure will rival military strength as a source of international power in the coming decade.
This compares military and territorial power with control over key technologies, networks, and the rules that make them work together.
Institutions lose legitimacy faster when a few powerful states write rules for everyone else.
Do institutions weaken faster when most states must follow rules they had little role in writing?
A global institution seems to work reasonably well, but rising powers increasingly reject its legitimacy. What best explains the problem?
Its governance is outdated
Voting weights, leadership access, and transparency rules have not adjusted enough to keep the institution credible.
Its social foundations are contested
The institution reflects particular norms and voices that others never fully accepted as neutral or universal.
Power shifted beneath it
States invoke legitimacy language when the institution serves them less well than before. The real story is changing power.
Its structure was unequal from the start
The institution sits inside a broader hierarchy of finance, production, and agenda-setting that procedural reform alone cannot fix.
A long-time rival democratizes, joins major institutions, and starts talking more cooperatively. How much should your threat assessment change?
Changes in regime type, elite discourse, and relationship history provide real evidence about future behavior.
Update it only cautiously
Capabilities and structural incentives still do most of the work. Political signals can reverse quickly.
Membership in shared institutions gives stronger evidence than declared values because it changes incentives and raises the cost of aggression.
The critical question is whether the new course is rooted in domestic coalitions strong enough to last beyond one leadership cycle.

A middle-income country pegs its currency to the dollar while banks and firms borrow heavily in dollars. Global interest rates rise, foreign lenders pull out, and emergency loans require spending cuts during a recession. Which factor best explains why the crisis is so hard to stop?
Choose the explanation that should guide the first response.
The currency peg and foreign-currency borrowing made an outside shock much worse. Rebuilding trust in domestic policy is the first condition for recovery.
Mixed crisis, mixed repair
Domestic policy choices and creditor leverage are both doing real work. Use temporary controls and renegotiate terms without abandoning the wider financial system.
The crisis exposes dependence on foreign-currency finance and creditor conditions. It will recur unless that dependence changes.
External finance sets the constraint, but domestic politics determines which workers, firms, and regions absorb the cuts.
A major ally keeps underspending on defense while relying on your guarantees. What is the most persuasive response?
Choose the response regardless of how you feel about the ally.
Free-riding corrodes credibility
Unequal burden undercuts collective defense and eventually weakens deterrence itself.
Measure shared capacity, not just shares
The real question is whether the alliance still delivers usable capability and coordination, not whether every member pays the same proportion.
The purpose is contested
Burden fights usually reflect a deeper disagreement about what the alliance is for and whose strategy it serves.
The guarantor is overextended
The first correction is to narrow commitments. An alliance that depends on unsustainable guarantees is badly designed.

After a border clash, a rival withdraws some troops and accepts a military hotline, but keeps new missiles in place and faces nationalist pressure at home. Which evidence should anchor your judgment of whether de-escalation will last?
Choose the evidence you would trust first when the signals point in different directions.
The missiles and remaining force posture matter most because they can be used regardless of promises or political language.
Compliance with the pullback and use of the hotline matter most because observable commitments are harder to fake than public messages.
The best clue is whether leaders can contain nationalist pressure and keep domestic support for the quieter course.
Status and relationship signals
Watch whether leaders stop describing the dispute as a test of national standing; that shift can change what the remaining weapons mean.
A coalition is debating export controls, investment screening, and shared technology standards against a rival. What is the main issue behind that push?
Choose what best explains the package as a whole.
Which best explains the package: slowing a rival, controlling chokepoints, limiting security rules, or preventing a new hierarchy?
Rules that restrict the sale of sensitive goods or technologies to certain foreign buyers.
Government review of foreign investments that may create security or strategic risks.
Groups of states or firms that coordinate technical rules among themselves instead of waiting for universal agreement.
Slow a rival's climb
The package is mainly about slowing a rival in sectors that feed military and industrial power.
The deeper issue is who controls the bottlenecks, data, and standards others cannot easily replace.
Keep the rules limited
The better case is for narrow allied rules that protect security without breaking the wider system.
Do not create a new hierarchy
The risk is a system where a few leading states write the rules and everyone else mainly absorbs the costs.
A middle power relies on one bloc for security and the other for trade. Which logic looks strongest from its side?
Answer from the middle power's position.
Lock in the security shield
Choose the security provider clearly before a crisis forces the decision under worse conditions.
Preserve room to maneuver by spreading risk across markets, partners, and supply lines.
Write rules with peers
Coalition-building with other middle powers is the best way to widen bargaining room and resist bloc pressure.
Use the country's pivotal position to extract concessions from both sides rather than declare a camp early.
A lower-income state is offered green-finance money tied to procurement and reform rules. Which logic looks strongest from its side?
Answer from the borrowing state's position.
Access to finance and policy credibility come first. Bargaining room is thin when fiscal stress is high.
The key issue is whether the deal locks the country into dependence and weakens local industry.
The best leverage comes from negotiating with peers that face the same terms rather than one by one.
Watch the home coalition
Even a fair external package fails if domestic winners and losers make it politically unsustainable.
An ally stages risky probes in disputed waters and asks for public backing. What should weigh most?
Choose the priority that should guide the response.
Hold the line on deterrence
Public backing deters more testing by the rival.
The bigger danger is being pulled into an escalation spiral by an ally's local gambles.
Build an off-ramp
The priority is monitoring, crisis rules, and quiet bargaining that let both sides step back.
Read the ally's politics
Before backing the move, ask whether the probe is being driven by domestic weakness or elite competition at home.
A government must choose between a cheap foreign digital stack and a costlier allied alternative. What should drive the choice?
Consider long-term exposure, not only the upfront price.
Which risk should lead: security exposure, long-term dependence, coordination with allies, or loss of autonomy?
The combined hardware, software, cloud services, and technical standards a digital system runs on.
The ability of systems from different countries or firms to work together reliably.
Choose the costlier stack if it lowers the risk that a rival can coerce or disable critical systems later.
Dependency and standards control
The central issue is who controls the standards, maintenance, and chokepoints once the system becomes hard to replace.
The best choice is the one that fits shared rules and technical coordination across trusted partners.
Avoid bloc lock-in
Turning every digital choice into a camp marker can narrow autonomy and harden a divided order.
Rising powers start building alternative banks, payment systems, and development forums. What is the deeper issue?
Choose why the alternatives are attractive, not your preferred reform.
Old governance stopped adjusting
The main problem is that existing institutions no longer give rising states enough voice, protection, or agenda-setting power.
Institutional conflict is downstream from changing material power. The argument over rules reflects a harder strategic transition.
States want room outside hierarchy
Alternative institutions give states options beyond credit, payment, and lending systems controlled by others.
Leaders want visible autonomy
Alternative institutions also help leaders show domestic audiences and partners that they are not permanently trapped inside systems dominated by others.
A nonaligned state condemns aggression but relies on the aggressor for cheap energy and fertilizer. Which logic looks strongest from its side?
Answer from the nonaligned state's position.
Defend the rule despite the cost
Absorbing real pain may be necessary if the state wants to defend the rule against conquest credibly.
Protect domestic stability first
Protect energy, food, and coalition stability at home; the government cannot sustain a line that breaks its domestic base.
Use the crisis to diversify
The stronger answer is to reduce structural dependence over time rather than swing instantly into a new dependency.
Condemn, but keep room to hedge
The state should oppose the breach without turning itself into an enforcement arm for someone else's wider strategy.

After a major insurgent attack, a Sahelian government is offered troops by its former colonial power. The force could help quickly, but earlier missions left resentment and weak local capacity. What should weigh most?
Answer from the Sahelian government's position.
Protect sovereignty and local control
Decline any arrangement that gives the outside force open-ended authority; short-term help is not worth renewed dependence.
Urgent danger can justify help
If civilians and state survival face extreme danger, tightly limited outside force can be justified despite the history.
Put regional actors in the lead
Accept help only through a mission whose aims, command, and exit terms are set mainly by neighboring states.
Judge the exit, not just the arrival
The decisive test is whether the mission leaves local forces and institutions stronger rather than creating another indefinite security dependency.
A rising power demands more voice in global rules while expanding military reach. What is the most persuasive reading?
Choose the explanation, not your preferred policy response.
It is mainly a power transition
As power shifts, the rising state pushes harder both militarily and institutionally because the old order serves it less well.
Recognition is the core issue
The state wants material room, but it also wants its status and authority claims treated as legitimate.
The sharper problem is that existing rules and leadership structures have not adjusted enough to absorb the new weight.
It is contesting hierarchy
The dispute is not only over voice. It is also over who controls finance, technology, and agenda-setting across the wider order.

A treaty ally finds that its main security partner has used force in clear breach of an agreement both signed. Suspending basing access would uphold the rule, but would also expose the ally to a nearby rival and threaten thousands of local jobs. What should govern its response?
Choose the priority that should govern the decision, not the easiest public message.
A treaty ally cannot make the agreement credible while continuing to enable a clear breach, even at real security and economic cost.
Do not trade away the country's deterrent position or domestic coalition for a response it cannot safely sustain.
Reduce dependence in stages
Set a timetable to diversify security support and the local economy before using basing access as leverage.
Separate condemnation from access
Condemn the breach and press for a settlement, but keep the base arrangement in place unless the violation widens.
A brutal war may end only if outside powers delay accountability and accept an unequal settlement. What is the deeper issue?
Choose the central tradeoff, not your preferred outcome.
Stop the harm now
An imperfect peace can still be defensible if it sharply reduces killing and buys time for political repair.
Hold the accountability line
If the hardest wars always suspend justice, the norm weakens exactly where future offenders are watching.
Sequence peace and justice
