Order among sovereign states

How can states maintain an international order without a world government? Bull examines the rules and practices that make a society of states possible, even when its members compete and sometimes go to war.
His account gives diplomacy, international law and the balance of power a place alongside conflict. It asks what holds an order together and whether alternatives to the states system would do better.
When rival governments keep diplomatic channels open during a crisis, what shared practices are they trying to preserve?
Explaining how an order survives does not settle whether it treats everyone fairly. Bull addresses order and justice as distinct questions.
Publisher description and contents for the fourth edition of the 1977 work; not a review of the full text.

Shared resources do not always require a choice between state control and private ownership. Ostrom studies how people who depend on the same forests, fisheries or water supplies can sometimes govern them together.

Governing the Commons compares arrangements that worked with ones that failed. The point is to understand the conditions that support cooperation, rather than assume that one form of ownership will solve every problem.
If several communities depend on the same water supply, who should help write its rules and how would they know whether those rules are being followed?
Success in one community does not establish that the same arrangement will work across countries or at a larger scale.
Publisher description and chapter contents for the 1990 book; not a review of every case study.
How ideas change as they travel
An idea promoted internationally does not arrive in an empty political landscape. Acharya asks how local actors adapt outside norms to beliefs and practices they already regard as legitimate.
His account of norm localization shifts attention from whether a region accepts or rejects an outside rule to how people reshape it. Local actors help determine what the rule comes to mean.
When a regional organization adopts an international principle, which parts change to fit local concerns, and who gets to decide?
Adaptation is not necessarily agreement with the original proposal. This account does not establish that every local practice is fair or that outside pressure never matters.
How Ideas Spread: Whose Norms Matter? Norm Localization and Institutional Change in Asian Regionalism
International Organization / Cambridge University Press
Published abstract of the 2004 article; a reading introduction, not a present-day policy profile.
A policy can improve a national total while leaving the poorest people no better off. Sen’s work asks what information we need to judge welfare, poverty and decisions made on behalf of society.
Counting everyone below a poverty line misses how far below it they are and how hardship is distributed. Sen also examines how collective decisions can take individual values and rights into account.
If a policy raises average income, what would you need to know about who gains and who loses before calling it a success?

A better measure makes a tradeoff easier to see; it does not choose the policy for us. This essay covers the research described by the Academy in 1998, not Sen’s later work or a position on a current dispute.
The Prize in Economic Sciences 1998: Social Choice, Welfare Distributions, and Poverty
Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences / NobelPrize.org
https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/1998/press-release/?app=true
The Academy’s 14 October 1998 explanation of Sen’s research contributions.

Cooperation need not depend on states becoming altruistic. Keohane asks how governments with competing interests can still make agreements worth keeping. Institutions matter when they change the practical conditions under which those governments bargain.

Repeated negotiations make reputation consequential. Shared information and monitoring help governments judge whether partners have kept an agreement; established procedures lower the cost of negotiating the next one. Reciprocity then has something observable to work with, even without a world government enforcing every promise.

This argument does not remove power from cooperation. A government may still reject a mutually beneficial arrangement if it fears that a rival will gain more from it. Institutional design therefore cannot be read as a guarantee of agreement.
International Institutions: Can Interdependence Work? (1998), PDF pp. 2–3, Theory and Reality / Challenges to Institutional Theory

Wendt questions a starting assumption shared by many debates about cooperation: that states arrive with fixed, self-interested identities. His 1994 argument asks whether interaction can change who states understand themselves to be, and therefore what they want.

If repeated interaction produces a collective identity, another state's interests can become part of how an actor defines its own. The proposed mechanism is a change in interests, beyond bargaining more efficiently over interests that stay fixed.

This is a hypothesis about how collective identities could form, not evidence that any particular rivalry will disappear. The article also raises a political cost: transnational authority could weaken the territorial basis of democratic accountability.
Collective Identity Formation and the International State (1994), abstract; full article not consulted for this note

Strange asks who can shape the conditions within which other people, firms and governments must act. A territorial map of states can miss authority exercised through markets, credit and control of knowledge.

Her structural account follows security, production, finance and knowledge rather than assuming that all consequential authority lies with governments. A relationship called interdependence may contain unequal dependence: one side has alternatives that the other lacks.

More rules do not necessarily mean more effective state authority. Strange distinguishes the quantity of regulation from governments' ability to perform basic functions. This is an argument from her 1996 preface, not a claim that states have vanished or a new assessment of today's balance of power.
The Retreat of the State (1996), preface, publisher preview PDF pp. 11–14

In his 2019 argument about international order, Mearsheimer links the limits of liberal projects to nationalism and great-power competition. The question is how far a shared order can reach when its political ambitions provoke resistance.

The published summary distinguishes an order that manages the world economy from smaller orders built around competing powers. Cooperation over some functions and security competition can therefore coexist in this account.

The predicted configuration is Mearsheimer's 2019 argument, not an established outcome or a current forecast by this project. The summary supports this narrow account; it does not establish how every institution or conflict will develop.
Bound to Fail (Spring 2019), Belfer Center published summary
